To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the changes in the relative root biomass in juvenile stands of afforestation species are primarily driven by ontogeny.

the changes in the relative root biomass allocation in juvenile stands of five fast-growing and slow-growing afforestation species are mainly driven by ontogeny but that the application of manuring and supplemental irrigation enhanced biomass production in all the species.
the changes in the relative allocation of biomass to roots in juvenile afforestation stands are mainly driven by ontogeny and not by variation in resource availability.

the effects of resource supply on the biomass allocation in fast-growing and slow-growing tree species in semi-arid conditions.
the effects of ontogeny, resource availability, and their interactions on biomass allocation in five afforestation species in a semi-arid climate.

the effects of resource allocation on biomass partitioning in fast-growing and slow-growing afforestation species in semi-arid conditions, with the objective of identifying the best species and silvicultural management practices for the rehabilitation of degraded land.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the biomass production in all the studied species was positively influenced by the application of manures and irrigation during both the dry season and the first and second rainy seasons, and that the biomass partitioning was controlled by ontogenetic changes.
silvicultural management aimed at increasing the availability of water and, particularly, nutrients enhances biomass production and biomass accumulation in all species.
the changes in the relative allocation to roots in the juvenile stands of the five semi-arid tree species were driven by ontogeny.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the changes in the relative root biomass allocation of the juvenile stands of the studied afforestation species are mainly driven by ontogeny and not by resource availability.

silvicultural management aimed at increasing resource availability can be a useful tool to enhance biomass production in all afforestation species, especially during the early stages of stand development.
the biomass production of the studied tree species is driven by ontogeny but can be enhanced by silvicultural management, particularly by the application of fertilizer and irrigation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
silvicultural management can be used to increase the biomass of fast-growing as well as slow-growing tree species.
silvicultural management, particularly the use of fertilizer and irrigation, is an effective tool to enhance the growth of fast-growing species in semi-arid areas.
silvicultural practices can increase the biomass production of afforestation species, which can be used to restore degraded land.
